reading.title: An email to a friend
reading.text:
Hi Emma,

Sorry I didn't come to your party on Saturday. On Friday night I had a terrible headache and a sore throat, and on Saturday morning I had a fever too. My mom took me to the doctor. She looked at my throat and my ears and said I had an infection. She gave me a prescription for some medicine. I have to take one pill three times a day, after meals. She also said I should drink a lot of water and stay in bed for two days.

I'm feeling much better now, but my back hurts because I stayed in bed all weekend! The doctor said I shouldn't go to the gym this week, so I'm going to watch movies at home. Can you tell me about the party? I want to see your photos.

Love,
Sofia

questions.q: Why didn't Sofia go to Emma's party?
questions.explain_es: Sofia dice que tenía dolor de cabeza, dolor de garganta y fiebre, o sea, estaba enferma.

questions.q: How often does Sofia take her medicine?
options: Three times a day, after meals
Two times a day, with water
questions.explain_es: El correo dice: one pill three times a day, after meals, es decir, tres veces al día después de comer.

questions.q: What did the doctor say Sofia shouldn't do this week?
questions.explain_es: La doctora dijo: you shouldn't go to the gym this week. Las otras opciones sí son cosas que debe hacer.

questions.q: Why does Sofia's back hurt?
options: She stayed in bed a lot.
questions.explain_es: Sofia explica que le duele la espalda porque se quedó en cama todo el fin de semana.

script.en: Good morning. What's the problem today?
Hi, doctor. I fell while I was playing soccer yesterday, and now my right wrist hurts a lot.
I see. Can you move your fingers?
Yes, but it hurts when I move my hand up and down.
Did you put any ice on it?
Yes, my sister gave me some ice last night, and I took two pills for the pain.
OK. I don't think it's broken, but we should take an X-ray to be sure.
Is it going to take a long time? I have to go to work at two.
No, about twenty minutes. And you shouldn't play soccer for three weeks.
Three weeks? Oh no, we have a big game next Saturday!
I'm sorry, but your health is more important. Are you allergic to any medicine?
No, I'm not.

questions.q: How did the man hurt himself?
options: He cut his hand at work.
He fell while he was playing soccer.
He hit his hand on a door.
questions.explain_es: El paciente dice: I fell while I was playing soccer yesterday.

questions.q: What part of his body hurts?
questions.explain_es: Dice claramente que le duele la muñeca derecha: my right wrist hurts a lot.

questions.q: What did he do last night?
options: He put ice on it and took some pills.

questions.q: What does the doctor want to do?

options: He can't play in a big game.
He is allergic to the medicine.
questions.explain_es: No puede jugar futbol por tres semanas y tiene un partido importante el próximo sábado.

use.q: I ___ a terrible headache right now.

use.q: The dentist checked all my ___.

use.q: Are you allergic ___ any food?
use.explain_es: En inglés se dice allergic to, con la preposición to.

use.q: Don't forget to ___ your medicine after dinner.
use.explain_es: Con medicinas y pastillas se usa take: take your medicine, take a pill.

use.q: I ___ off my bike yesterday and cut my knee.

writing.prompt_es: Escribe un correo a tu maestra de inglés, la Sra. López. Dile que no puedes ir a clase mañana, explica qué síntomas tienes, cuenta qué te dijo el doctor y pregúntale por la tarea. Escribe de 35 a 60 palabras.
writing.prompt_en: You can't go to your English class tomorrow. Write an email to your teacher, Ms. Lopez. In your email: say that you can't go to class, explain how you feel, say what the doctor told you to do, and ask about the homework. Write 35–60 words.

Dear Ms. Lopez,

reading.title: The trip where everything went wrong
reading.text:
Last month I flew from Guadalajara to Chicago for a work conference, and almost everything that could go wrong did. First, my flight was delayed three hours because of a storm, so I missed my connection in Dallas. The airline staff were very helpful, though. They booked me on the next flight and gave me a voucher for dinner. When I finally landed in Chicago, it was after midnight, and my suitcase wasn't on the baggage carousel. I filled out a form at the lost baggage desk and took a taxi to the hotel.

At the front desk, the receptionist couldn't find my reservation. I showed her the confirmation email, and she realized the booking was under my company's name, not mine. She apologized and gave me a free upgrade to a suite on the twelfth floor, with a view of the lake.

The next morning, the airline called to say my bag was on its way. It arrived at the hotel before lunch, so I only had to wear the same shirt for one day. My advice? Always pack a change of clothes and your charger in your carry-on. You never know when you might need them.

questions.q: Why did the writer miss her connecting flight?
options: She arrived late at the airport.
questions.explain_es: El primer vuelo se retrasó tres horas por una tormenta, por eso perdió la conexión en Dallas.

questions.q: What did the airline give her in Dallas?
questions.explain_es: La aerolínea le dio a voucher for dinner, un vale para cenar.

questions.q: Why couldn't the receptionist find the reservation at first?
options: It was under the name of her company.
It was for a different date.
questions.explain_es: La reservación estaba a nombre de su empresa, no al suyo: under my company's name.

questions.q: What happened to her suitcase?
options: It was delivered to the hotel the next day.
It stayed in Dallas for a week.
She picked it up at the airport.
questions.explain_es: La aerolínea llamó en la mañana y la maleta llegó al hotel antes de la comida.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the writer's advice at the end?
options: To recommend the hotel in Chicago
To tell people to avoid connecting flights
To suggest keeping important things in your hand luggage
questions.explain_es: Recomienda llevar ropa extra y el cargador en el equipaje de mano (carry-on) por si pasa algo.

script.en: Good evening, welcome to the Bayview Hotel. Are you checking in?
Yes, I have a reservation under Ramírez. Two nights, a double room.
Let me see... Yes, here it is. Room 418, on the fourth floor. Breakfast is served from six thirty to ten in the restaurant.
Great. Could you tell me what time checkout is?
It's at eleven. If you need a late checkout, it's twenty dollars extra.
That's fine, I'll let you know. Oh, and would you mind calling a taxi for me tomorrow at seven? I have a meeting downtown.
No, not at all. The taxi will be waiting at the main entrance.
Thank you. One more thing, is the Wi-Fi free?
Yes, it is. The password is on your key card holder. The elevators are just behind you, on the left.
Perfect. Thanks so much for your help.

use.explain_es: Registrarse en el aeropuerto o en el hotel es check in.

use.q: In the US, the ground floor is called the ___ floor.
use.explain_es: En Estados Unidos la planta baja es el first floor.

use.explain_es: Una queja amable suele empezar con I'm sorry, but y luego el problema.

writing.prompt_es: Vas a viajar a San Diego. Escribe un correo al hotel para reservar una habitación. Incluye: las fechas y el tipo de habitación, una petición especial, una pregunta sobre el desayuno y una pregunta sobre el transporte desde el aeropuerto. Escribe de 70 a 100 palabras.
writing.prompt_en: You are planning a trip to San Diego. Write an email to a hotel to book a room. In your email: give the dates and type of room, make a special request, ask about breakfast, and ask about transportation from the airport. Write 70–100 words.
writing.model_answer:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I would like to book a double room for three nights, from June 12 to June 15. The reservation should be under the name Ana Torres. Could you give me a quiet room on a high floor, if possible? Thank you in advance for your help.

Best regards,

reading.title: A message about future plans
reading.text:
Hi Marco,

Thanks for your message! I can't believe we're graduating in six weeks. You asked about my plans, so here they are. I'm not going to look for a job right away. Instead, I'm going to spend three months in Canada. I've already found a language school in Toronto, and I'm flying there on August 2nd. My classes start on the 5th, so I'll have a few days to get to know the city first.

After Canada, I'm planning to come back to Monterrey and work at my uncle's architecture firm. He says I'll probably start as an assistant, but I don't mind. Hopefully, by this time next year, I'll have saved enough money to buy a car.

What about you? Your sister told me you might move to Mexico City. Is that true? If you're free next weekend, would you like to come over for a barbecue? A few people from our class are coming on Saturday at four. I really hope you can make it. I'm looking forward to seeing you!

Take care,
Daniela

questions.q: What is Daniela going to do right after she graduates?
questions.explain_es: Dice que no va a buscar trabajo de inmediato; primero se va tres meses a Canadá a una escuela de idiomas.

questions.q: Why is Daniela flying to Toronto on August 2nd?
options: Because her classes start that day
To have some time to explore the city before classes
questions.explain_es: Sus clases empiezan el 5, así que llega antes para conocer la ciudad unos días.

questions.q: What does she say about the job at the architecture firm?
options: She will start before she goes to Canada.
She doesn't want to work there.
She will probably start in a junior position.
She is going to be the manager.
questions.explain_es: Su tío dice que probablemente empezará como asistente, es decir, en un puesto básico.

questions.q: What does Daniela hope to do by next year?
options: Save enough money for a car
questions.explain_es: Usa el futuro perfecto: by this time next year, I'll have saved enough money to buy a car.

questions.q: What do we know about Marco's plans?
options: He is going to work with Daniela.
He is definitely coming to the barbecue.
He has decided to move to Canada.
He may move to Mexico City.
questions.explain_es: Daniela usa might: you might move to Mexico City. Es una posibilidad, no algo seguro.

script.en: Hey, Luis, what are you doing this Saturday?
In the morning I'm helping my dad paint the kitchen. Why?
There's a jazz festival in the park. Would you like to come with us in the afternoon?
I'd love to, but I think the painting will take all day. Maybe Sunday?
The festival is only on Saturday, unfortunately. How about meeting for dinner after you finish, then?
That sounds great. I'll probably be done by seven.
Perfect. I'm going to book a table at that new Korean place on Juárez Street.
Oh, I've heard it's really good. Should I invite Carla?
Sure, but she might be busy. She said she's working late this weekend.
OK, I'll text her tonight. And don't worry, I won't be late this time, I promise.

options: Helping his dad paint the kitchen

questions.q: Why can't Luis go to the festival?
options: He thinks he'll be busy all day.

questions.q: What time does Luis think he will finish?

To invite Carla to the festival

use.q: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.
use.explain_es: Cuando hay una evidencia que ves ahora, usa going to: it's going to rain.

use.q: The phone is ringing. Don't worry, I ___ answer it.
use.explain_es: Para decisiones tomadas en el momento se usa will: I'll answer it.

use.q: I'm looking forward to ___ you next week.
use.explain_es: Después de look forward to va el verbo con -ing, porque to aquí es preposición.

use.q: Would you like ___ to the movies tonight?
use.explain_es: Después de would you like va to + verbo: would you like to go?

use.q: How about ___ pizza tonight?
use.explain_es: Después de how about el verbo va con -ing: how about ordering?

use.q: My train ___ at 7:45 tomorrow morning, so I need to get up early.
use.explain_es: Para horarios oficiales como trenes o vuelos se usa el presente simple: the train leaves at 7:45.

use.q: I'm not sure yet, but I ___ go to the beach this weekend.
use.explain_es: Might expresa posibilidad y va con el verbo base sin to: I might go.

use.q: This time tomorrow, I ___ on a beach in Cancún.
use.explain_es: Para una acción en progreso en un momento del futuro se usa will be + -ing.

use.q: By the end of the year, we ___ the new house.
use.explain_es: Para algo que ya estará terminado antes de cierto momento se usa will have + participio.

use.q: Sorry, I can't. I ___ my grandparents on Friday. We arranged it last week.
use.explain_es: Para planes ya acordados con alguien se usa el presente continuo: I'm visiting my grandparents.

writing.prompt_es: Tu amigo estadounidense Jake te escribió: ¿Qué vas a hacer en las vacaciones de verano? Me gustaría visitarte. Contéstale: cuéntale tus planes, invítalo, sugiere algo que pueden hacer juntos y pregúntale cuándo puede venir. Escribe de 70 a 100 palabras.
writing.prompt_en: Your American friend Jake has written to you: What are you going to do this summer? I'd love to visit you! Write an email to Jake. In your email: tell him about your plans, invite him, suggest something you could do together, and ask when he can come. Write 70–100 words.
writing.model_answer:
Hi Jake,

Great to hear from you! This summer I'm going to work at my aunt's café in the mornings, because I want to save some money. In August, my family is going to spend a week in Oaxaca. Why don't you come and visit us in July? We could go hiking in the mountains, or I could show you the best taco places in my city. I'm sure you'll love it. When is your vacation? Let me know soon so I can tell my parents.

See you soon,
Andrés

Una invitación clara (Why don't you... / Would you like to...)
Una sugerencia de actividad con could o how about
Una pregunta sobre cuándo puede venir
Saludo y despedida informales

reading.title: From the office to the ocean
reading.text:
Ricardo Fuentes has worked as a diving instructor in Bacalar for six years, but his life used to be very different. 'I used to sit in an office in Mexico City for ten hours a day,' he says. 'I was an accountant, and I was bored all the time.'

In 2017 he took a vacation in Quintana Roo and tried scuba diving for the first time. 'It was the best day of my life. I had never felt so free,' he remembers. Six months later, he quit his job, sold his car and moved to the coast.

The first year was hard. He had to get used to earning much less money, and he didn't speak much English, which most of the tourists use. But he has been taking online English classes since he arrived, and his English has improved a lot. 'It's the first time I've really loved my job,' he says.

Has he ever thought about going back? 'Never. My friends from the office have come to visit me, and some of them are jealous!' He has taught more than two thousand students so far, and he has just opened his own diving school.

questions.explain_es: Ricardo dice: I was an accountant, era contador.

questions.q: When did he try scuba diving for the first time?
options: Six years ago, in Mexico City
questions.explain_es: En 2017 se fue de vacaciones a Quintana Roo y buceó por primera vez.

questions.q: What was difficult during his first year?
options: Earning less money and speaking English
questions.explain_es: Tuvo que acostumbrarse a ganar menos dinero y casi no hablaba inglés.

questions.q: What has Ricardo done recently?
options: He has opened his own diving school.
He has gone back to Mexico City.
questions.explain_es: Just significa acabar de: he has just opened his own diving school.

questions.q: How do some of his old colleagues feel about his new life?
options: They wish they had a life like his.
questions.explain_es: Dice que algunos están jealous, celosos o con envidia, o sea, les gustaría tener su vida.

listening.title: Catching up with an old friend

script.en: Mariana! I haven't seen you in ages. How have you been?
Hi, Tom! I've been great, thanks. I've just come back from Japan, actually.
Japan? Wow! How long were you there?
Three weeks. It's the first time I've been to Asia. I went to Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
Did you eat real ramen? I've always wanted to try it there.
Oh, yes, almost every day! What about you? Are you still working at the bank?
No, I quit last year. I've been working as a web designer since January.
That's a big change! Do you like it?
I love it. I used to hate Mondays, but now I don't mind them at all.
Good for you! Hey, has your brother gone back to Canada?
Yes, he went back in March. He's been living in Vancouver for almost five years now.

questions.q: How long was Mariana in Japan?
questions.explain_es: Ella responde: Three weeks.

questions.q: What is true about Mariana's trip?
options: It was her first time in Asia.
She had been to Asia many times.
questions.explain_es: Dice: It's the first time I've been to Asia.

questions.q: When did Tom start his current job?
questions.explain_es: Tom dice: I've been working as a web designer since January. Renunció al banco el año pasado.

questions.q: How does Tom feel about Mondays now?

questions.q: Where is Tom's brother now?
questions.explain_es: Su hermano regresó a Canadá y vive en Vancouver desde hace casi cinco años.

use.q: Have you ___ been to Oaxaca?
use.explain_es: Para preguntar por experiencias de vida se usa ever: Have you ever been...?

use.q: I haven't finished my homework ___.
use.explain_es: Yet va al final en negativas y preguntas: I haven't finished yet.

use.q: We have lived in this apartment ___ 2019.
use.explain_es: Since se usa con el momento en que empezó algo (since 2019); for con periodos (for five years).

use.q: I ___ that movie last weekend.
use.explain_es: Con una fecha terminada como last weekend se usa past simple: I saw.

use.q: Ana isn't here. She has ___ to the supermarket, but she'll be back soon.
use.explain_es: Has gone to significa que se fue y sigue allá. Has been to significa que fue y ya regresó.

use.q: I've ___ waiting for the bus for forty minutes!
use.explain_es: El present perfect continuous se forma con have + been + -ing: I've been waiting.

use.q: It's the first time I ___ sushi.
use.explain_es: Después de It's the first time va present perfect: It's the first time I've eaten...

use.q: When I was a kid, I ___ play outside every afternoon.
use.explain_es: Used to + verbo base habla de hábitos del pasado que ya no ocurren.

use.q: It took me months to get used to ___ up at 5 a.m.
use.explain_es: Get used to significa acostumbrarse y va seguido de un verbo con -ing.

use.q: My English has ___ a lot since I started this course.
use.explain_es: En present perfect se usa have/has + participio: has improved.

writing.prompt_es: Viste este anuncio en una revista en inglés: Buscamos artículos. La mejor experiencia de mi vida. ¿Qué pasó? ¿Por qué fue tan especial? ¿Cómo te cambió? Escribe tu artículo de 70 a 100 palabras.
writing.prompt_en: You see this announcement in an English-language magazine: Articles wanted! The best experience of my life. What happened? Why was it so special? How has it changed you? Write your article in 70–100 words.
writing.model_answer:
A Morning I Will Never Forget

I've traveled to many places, but the best experience of my life happened close to home. Two years ago, my friends and I climbed the Nevado de Toluca at night to see the sunrise. It was freezing, and I almost gave up twice. When the sun finally appeared over the crater lake, everyone went silent. I had never seen anything so beautiful. Since then, I've climbed four more mountains, and I've learned that I'm stronger than I thought. Have you ever tried something that scared you? You should!
checklist_es: Un título atractivo
Cuentas qué pasó usando past simple con fechas o momentos concretos
Explicas por qué fue especial
Explicas cómo te cambió usando present perfect (Since then, I've...)
Hablas directamente al lector, por ejemplo con una pregunta

reading.title: Why I love quiet weekends
reading.text:
Most of my friends think I'm boring because I'd rather stay home on Saturday nights than go to a club. To be honest, I used to feel embarrassed about it. Now I don't care. For me, a quiet evening with a good book is far more relaxing than a noisy party, and it's much cheaper too.

Don't get me wrong, I'm not lonely. I just enjoy being alone sometimes. My sister, Paola, disagrees with me. She says going out is the best way to meet people, and she gets bored if she spends more than one night at home. We argue about it all the time, but we both agree on one thing: the worst plan is a night out with people you don't like.

Personally, I think the important thing is to know yourself. If parties make you nervous, there's no need to force yourself. And if staying home makes you anxious, go out! Last weekend I tried a new board game café near my house. It was quieter than a bar but a lot more fun than my sofa. Was it worth it? Definitely. I'd go again.

questions.q: How did the writer feel about staying home in the past?
questions.explain_es: El autor dice: I used to feel embarrassed about it, antes le daba pena.

questions.q: What does the writer say about being alone?
options: They only do it on weekdays.
It makes them feel sad and lonely.
They enjoy it sometimes, but they aren't lonely.
They hate it, but it's cheaper.

reading.title: What recruiters really notice
reading.text:
After fifteen years as a recruiter for a logistics company in Monterrey, Verónica Salas has interviewed more than three thousand candidates. Surprisingly, she says the people who get hired are rarely the ones with the most impressive résumés.

'A résumé gets you through the door, but it doesn't get you the job,' she explains. 'What I'm really listening for is how candidates talk about their mistakes.' According to Salas, many applicants freeze when asked about a project that went wrong, or they simply blame their former boss. The candidates who impress her admit what happened and explain what they would have done differently if they had known more at the time.

She is equally direct about follow-up emails. In her experience, candidates who send a short thank-you message within twenty-four hours are far more likely to be remembered. However, she warns against sounding desperate. 'One email is professional. Three emails in a week is a red flag.'

Salary negotiation is another area where people make avoidable errors. Rather than naming a figure too early, she recommends asking about the full package first, including benefits and opportunities for training. 'If you accept the first offer without asking a single question, I start to wonder how you'll negotiate with our clients.'

Her final piece of advice may sound obvious, but she insists it is ignored more often than not: research the company before the interview. Nothing ends a conversation faster, she says, than a candidate asking what exactly the company does.

reading.title: Logging off: one week without social media
reading.text:
Last month, after realizing I'd checked my phone over a hundred times in a single day, I decided to try something drastic: one full week without social media, streaming or unnecessary apps. I kept my phone for calls and texts, since my job requires it, but I deleted everything else and asked my team to email me instead.

The first two days were genuinely uncomfortable. I kept reaching for my phone without thinking, and I felt anxious that I was missing something important. By Wednesday, though, something shifted. I finished a novel I had abandoned months ago, and I noticed I was sleeping better, probably because I was no longer scrolling in bed until midnight.

Not everything was positive. I missed a friend's birthday dinner because the invitation was only posted in a group chat, and I felt terrible when she mentioned it. It made me realize how much of our social lives now depends on platforms that most of us claim to dislike.

When the week ended, I didn't go back to my old habits completely. I've reinstalled only two apps, and I've turned off almost all notifications. I also back up my photos manually once a week instead of letting my phone do it automatically, which has made me more aware of how much data I generate.

Would I recommend the experiment? Yes, but with one warning: tell your friends first.

options: Her friends asked her to keep it.

writing.prompt_en: In your English class you have been talking about technology. Now your teacher has asked you to write an essay. Technology has made our lives more stressful, not easier. Do you agree? Notes: write about 1. work, 2. relationships, 3. your own idea. Write 120–160 words.
writing.model_answer:
It is often said that technology was supposed to make life easier, yet many people feel more stressed than ever. In my view, this is only partly true.

On the one hand, technology has changed the way we work. Thanks to email and video calls, many people can work remotely, which saves time and money. However, it also means we are always available, and it is hard to disconnect when your boss can text you at ten at night.

On the other hand, social media has affected our relationships. It allows us to stay in touch with friends who live far away, but it can also make us compare our lives with others and feel anxious.

In conclusion, I believe technology itself is not the problem. The real issue is how we use it, so we need clear limits, such as turning off notifications after work.

reading.title: From market stall to online store
reading.text:
When Lucía Pérez lost her office job in 2020, she had enough savings to cover three months of rent and very little else. What she did have was her grandmother's recipe for mole and a small kitchen in Puebla. Four years later, her company ships jars of sauce to customers across Mexico and the southern United States.

'At first I sold at a weekend market, and I barely broke even,' she admits. 'After paying for ingredients, the stall and transportation, there was almost no profit.' Instead of giving up, she started tracking every peso in a simple spreadsheet. She discovered that her most popular product was also the one with the lowest margin, so she raised its price slightly. To her surprise, sales hardly dropped.

The real turning point came when she began selling online. Shipping costs were a constant headache, and an early batch of jars broke in transit, leading to a wave of complaints and refund requests. Rather than arguing with customers, she apologized publicly, replaced every order free of charge and redesigned her packaging. 'It cost me a fortune that month,' she says, 'but many of those customers are still loyal today.'

Lucía has turned down two offers from investors who wanted a majority stake in the business. 'They were generous,' she says, 'but I'd rather grow slowly and keep control.' Her advice to future entrepreneurs is refreshingly practical: 'Know your numbers before you worry about your logo.'

Our contracts with suppliers have not been reviewed for three years. I recommend negotiating new terms or asking for discounts on larger orders. Several competitors have already done this successfully.

Travel
Many business trips could easily be replaced by video calls, which would save both money and time.

Recommendation
I would suggest starting with a review of our supplier contracts, as this would have the biggest impact on our profit in the shortest time.

reading.title: Review: The Salt Road, season one
reading.text:
When it was announced that the bestselling novel The Salt Road would be adapted into a series, fans of the book were nervous. Novels that depend so heavily on a narrator's inner thoughts rarely survive the move to the screen. I'm pleased to report that, for the most part, those worries were unnecessary.

The eight-episode first season, which was filmed almost entirely on the coast of Baja California, follows Inés, a marine biologist who returns to her hometown after her father disappears at sea. Newcomer Camila Ríos is outstanding in the lead role, and she carries scenes that could easily have felt slow. The supporting cast is solid, although her brother's character is so underwritten that you sometimes forget he's there.

Visually, the show is stunning. The ocean feels both beautiful and threatening, and the soundtrack, composed by a local folk musician, is used sparingly and to great effect. I found myself looking up the lyrics of the opening song after the first episode.

Where the series stumbles is in its final two episodes. The writers have added a subplot about a corrupt politician that isn't in the book, and it feels rushed and out of place. Readers who loved the novel's ambiguous ending may also be frustrated that everything is explained so neatly here.

Still, these are minor complaints. If you're into slow-burning mysteries, I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. A second season has already been confirmed.

reading.title: In defense of changing your mind
reading.text:
There is a peculiar contempt reserved, in public life especially, for people who change their minds. Politicians are accused of flip-flopping; executives who reverse a strategy are seen as weak. Yet the ability to revise one's views in light of new evidence is arguably the defining feature of a mature thinker, not a flaw to be concealed.

Part of the problem, I'd argue, lies in how we frame disagreement. Debates are staged as contests to be won, and conceding a point is treated as losing face. Despite decades of research showing that people rarely abandon a belief when confronted aggressively, we persist in arguing as if volume were a substitute for persuasion. Had we been taught to see a well-made counterargument as a gift rather than an attack, many of our public conversations would look quite different.

None of this is to suggest that every opinion should be held loosely. Some convictions are rightly firm, and someone who changes position with every passing trend is not so much open-minded as unanchored. The distinction lies in the reason for the change. Shifting because a more compelling piece of evidence has emerged is intellectual honesty; shifting because it has become socially convenient is something else entirely.

What, then, would a healthier culture look like? For a start, it would make room for phrases such as 'I hadn't considered that' or 'I may have been wrong' without treating them as admissions of defeat. It would reward leaders who explain why they reconsidered, rather than punishing them for having done so. Eventually, perhaps, we might come to regard the person who has never changed their mind not as admirably consistent, but as someone who has simply stopped paying attention.

questions.q: What is the writer's main argument?
options: All opinions should be held loosely.
Revising your views in response to evidence is a sign of maturity.
Politicians should never change their minds.
questions.explain_es: La idea central es que cambiar de opinión ante nueva evidencia es señal de un pensador maduro, no un defecto.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about arguing aggressively?
options: It has only recently become common.
It is the most effective way to persuade.
It seldom succeeds in changing people's beliefs.
questions.explain_es: Menciona investigaciones que muestran que la gente casi nunca abandona una creencia cuando la confrontan de forma agresiva.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, what distinction does the writer make?
options: Between changing views for good reasons and for convenience
questions.explain_es: Distingue entre cambiar por evidencia más convincente (honestidad intelectual) y cambiar porque es socialmente conveniente.

questions.explain_es: Por el contexto, alguien que cambia con cada moda no tiene principios firmes que lo sostengan, como un barco sin ancla.

questions.q: What does the final sentence imply about people who never change their minds?
options: They may no longer be engaging with new information.
They have better arguments than others.
They deserve admiration for their consistency.
questions.explain_es: Es una inferencia irónica: quien nunca cambia de opinión quizá simplemente dejó de prestar atención.

writing.prompt_es: Después de un debate en clase, tu profesor te pide un ensayo sobre esta pregunta: ¿Deberían las ciudades prohibir los coches en sus centros históricos? Elige dos de estos aspectos y explica cuál es más importante, con razones: la calidad del aire, los negocios locales, la vida de los residentes. Usa conectores formales y lenguaje matizado. Escribe de 180 a 220 palabras.
writing.prompt_en: Your class has watched a panel discussion about cities banning cars from their historic centers. You have made the notes below. Notes: air quality, local businesses, residents' quality of life. Write an essay discussing two of the points in your notes. Explain which point you think is more important, giving reasons to support your opinion. Write 180–220 words.
writing.model_answer:
In recent years, a number of cities have chosen to close their historic centers to private cars. While the policy is often controversial, I would argue that its benefits clearly outweigh its drawbacks.

The most compelling argument in its favor concerns air quality. Historic centers tend to have narrow streets in which pollution accumulates, and the evidence linking traffic fumes to respiratory illness is difficult to dispute. Removing cars would not only make these areas healthier but would also help preserve old buildings, which are gradually damaged by exhaust.

Opponents frequently claim that local businesses would suffer if customers could no longer drive to them. This concern is understandable, yet experience elsewhere suggests that it is somewhat exaggerated. Pedestrian streets generally attract more visitors, who tend to stay longer and spend more. Indeed, in several European cities, shop owners who initially protested are now among the plan's strongest supporters.

That said, such a ban can only succeed if it is accompanied by reliable public transport and adequate access for residents, deliveries and people with disabilities.

On balance, therefore, I believe air quality is the decisive factor. Provided that the transition is managed carefully, banning cars from historic centers is a measure that cities should seriously consider.

Conectores formales (however, yet, therefore, that said, despite)
Lenguaje matizado (arguably, somewhat, tend to, I would argue)
Conclusión que dice cuál aspecto es más importante y por qué
